# [TITLE C20]

Anonymous authors

Paper under double-blind review

# ABSTRACT

Graph-based RAG organizes fragmented text into explicit knowledge structures for retrieval through entities, relations, and article summaries. However, directly bringing graph-based RAG to smartphones creates a mismatch between cloud-oriented graph methods and mobile constraints: compact on-device models are more likely to miss entities, predict incorrect relations, or merge distinct entity mentions, while multi-level graph summaries require frequent, large-context LLM invocations. We build [NAME C20], to the best of our knowledge, the first graph-based RAG framework end-to-end deployed on commercial smartphones. [NAME C20] combines MRGraph, a two-layer mobile graph that preserves entities, relations, and source paragraphs; EvoNER, which incrementally learns unseen entity types and locally updates the graph; and ATPlanner, which uses one LLM call to guide hybrid retrieval under a fixed budget. On real smartphones, [NAME C20] outperforms prior mobile RAG baselines by up to 22.4 points in correctness, constructs knowledge graphs 13.77× faster, and consumes only 1.36% of the energy compared with the latest lightweight methods. Each higher-level node summarizes connected lower-level nodes to locate a semantic region, but on-device LLMs have limited usable context and weaker abstraction capabilities. Repeated summarization can introduce descriptions unsupported by source documents while incurring prohibitive latency and energy overhead due to frequent invocations. A natural question is whether reducing the number of LLM invocations by limiting GraphRAG to two hierarchy levels can support mobile deployment. Our experiments on a subset of MultiHopQA show that this two-level GraphRAG variant only achieves an F1-score of 6.79% and requires about 37 182 s for on-device graph construction. This is substantially lower than original GraphRAG with an F1-score of 25.26%. Thus, reducing the number of levels alone can not address either inaccurate on-device knowledge extraction or LLM-based summary costs. ## 2.2 PREVIOUS RAG METHODS

**Vector-based RAG** encodes document chunks into dense embeddings and retrieves the top-$k$ most similar chunks for each query (Karpukhin et al., 2020). This design scales well, but each chunk is retrieved independently which has no explicit mechanism to chain evidence across documents.

**Graph-based RAG** addresses this by extracting entities and relations from documents and organizing them into entity-relation graphs that make cross-document connections explicit (Edge et al., 2024; Peng et al., 2025). The core intuition is that a graph exposes the *topology* of knowledge, who is connected to whom through what relationship, enabling retrieval to follow structured paths rather than relying solely on semantic similarity.

GraphRAG first splits documents into chunks and invokes an LLM on each chunk to extract entities and relations. Extracted elements are assembled into a graph $\mathcal{G} = (\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{R})$. A defining characteristic is the subsequent construction of a multi-level community hierarchy via Leiden

A lightweight named entity recognizer is cheaper, but is restricted to a fixed label space and cannot reliably process newly emerging entity types (Zhang et al., 2024). ### 4.1 SETUP

We use compact LLM backbones from the Qwen3 (Qwen Team, 2025) and Ministral3 (Liu et al., 2026a) families, and compare against two groups of baselines: (1) LLM-only models without retrieval, and (2) RAG methods including Naïve RAG (Lewis et al., 2020), GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024), InstructRAG (Wei et al., 2025), StableRAG (Zhang et al., 2026), TruthfulRAG (Liu et al., 2026b), xRAG (Cheng et al., 2024), and MiniRAG (Fan et al., 2025), for fair comparison.

[NAME C20] and NaïveRAG are executed entirely on real smartphones. Due to unacceptable graph construction time cost by LLM invocations other RAG methods are simulated in a cloud environment with same experiment settings. To demonstrate the on-device feasibility of [NAME C20], we compared it with MiniRAG's graph construction process on smartphones. Details are provided in Appendix A.

# AI USE STATEMENT

In this work, we used generative AI tools to assist with code implementation, generate supervision for retrieval-planner training, and assess the correctness of answers produced by the evaluated RAG systems. Specifically, Claude Opus 4.6 generated planner-training supervision, which underwent rule-based filtering and manual verification, and Claude Haiku 4.5 served as an LLM judge under the protocol described in Appendix C. We did not use generative AI tools to conduct the preliminary literature review, formulate the proposed methodology, or design the experiments. These activities, together with the execution of experimental tests, were carried out by the human authors. Additionally, we used generative AI tools to edit the manuscript for language and readability. The authors reviewed the AI-assisted manuscript edits and code, tested the implementation, and manually checked a sample of the LLM-generated judgments. **Graph-based RAG systems.** Graph-based RAG systems organize text into graph structures for multi-hop evidence composition (Edge et al., 2024; Han et al., 2025). Representative systems use community summaries, lightweight graph construction, or iterative graph navigation (Guo et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2025). These designs are effective in server-side settings, but their deep LLM-generated semantic levels are difficult to construct, update, and traverse on smartphones. [NAME C20] therefore uses a shallow graph memory that keeps the abstraction needed for search and the provenance needed for grounded reasoning.

Qi Zhan, Yile Wang \( ^{*} \) , Hui Huang

CSSE, Shenzhen University

qzhan65@gmail.com, wangyile@szu.edu.cn, hhzhiyan@gmail.com

## Abstract

Named entity recognition (NER) is evolving from a sequence labeling task into a generative paradigm with the rise of large language models (LLMs). We conduct a systematic evaluation of open-source LLMs on both flat and nested NER tasks. We investigate several research questions including the performance gap between generative NER and traditional NER models, the impact of output formats, whether LLMs rely on memorization, and the preservation of general capabilities after fine-tuning. Through experiments across eight LLMs of varying scales and four standard NER datasets, we find that: (1) With parameter-efficient fine-tuning and structured formats like inline bracketed or XML, open-source LLMs achieve performance competitive with traditional encoder-based models and surpass decoder-based LLMs with in-context learning techniques; (2) The NER capability of LLMs stems from instruction-following and generative power, no

the aforementioned studies test the performance of closed-source models like ChatGPT (OpenAI, 2022) for zero-shot NER, and there is currently a lack of systematic investigation into the effectiveness of fine-tuned open-source LLMs, such as advanced LLaMA (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Qwen (Yang et al., 2025), Granite (IBM Research, 2025) and Gemma (Gemma Team, 2025) models. Specifically, we seek to examine whether generative LLMs represent a reliable approach and whether there is a performance gap compared to traditional pre-trained model methods on both flat and nested NER tasks.

How do different output formats affect the performance of LLMs in generative NER? The performance of LLMs is highly sensitive to the specific instructions given by users. While recent studies have touched upon format designs (Kim et al., 2024; Lv et al., 2025), we systematically explore a more diverse set of output templates as a supplement to the aforementioned work and investigate their specific impact on NER performance. Specifically, we design five distinct output formats (Inline Bracketed, Inline XML, Category-grouped JSON, Occurrence-based JSON, and Offset-based JSON) to compare their impact and investigate whether the performance of different models remains consistent across these v

### 3.2 Results

The results for flat and nested NER are shown in Table 3 and Table 4, respectively. We report single-run Micro-F1 scores in the main text and provide the complete Precision, Recall, and F1 results in Appendix H. The main findings are as follows:

The output format has a decisive impact on the performance of generative NER. Among the five output formats, the Inline Bracketed and Inline XML formats achieve the best average performance across all LLMs, with average F1 scores of 91.91/82.85 and 91.71/82.67 on flat and nested NER. Both inline formats consistently outperform the JSON-based formats (90.78/81.69, 91.17/80.07 and 53.91/34.53). These results indicate that clear, structured, natural-language-like inline outputs are more conducive to helping LLMs understand and generate accurate entity information, whereas formats requiring concluding the whole information all at once and precise character-offset calculations are poorly suited to the text-generation nature of LLMs, leading to a sharp decline in performance.

## 1 Introduction

Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing, widely used in downstream applications such as relation extraction, knowledge graph construction, information retrieval, and question answering systems. As a typical sequence labeling task, approaches based on traditional auto-encoding pre-trained models have achieved strong results [Devlin et al. (2019)](#bib.bib4); [Li et al. (2020a)](#bib.bib7); [Lu et al. (2022)](#bib.bib28); [Yan et al. (2023)](#bib.bib24).

![Refer to caption](2601.17898v1/intro.png)

The development of generative pre-trained models [Radford et al. (2019)](#bib.bib36); [Lewis et al. (2020)](#bib.bib5) and large language models (LLMs; [Brown et al., 2020](#bib.bib29); [OpenAI, 2022](#bib.bib31); [OpenAI, 2023](#bib.bib30); [DeepSeek-AI, 2024](#bib.bib32)) is gradually shifting traditional NER task toward a unified generative paradigm. As shown in Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Assessment of Generative Named Entity Recognition in the Era of Large Language Models"), LLMs sequentially generate user-provided sentences along with their corresponding entity labels in textual form. This approach demonstrates strong interactivity, generalization, and user-friendliness. Recent studies

### 3.1 Settings

Instructions and Output Format. Prompt design is crucial for LLM fine-tuning. It mainly includes the design of instructions primarily used to specify the tasks the model needs to complete, and the output format used for answer generation, extraction, and validation. For the complete instructions, we provide them in Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Full Instructions for Different Datasets ‣ Assessment of Generative Named Entity Recognition in the Era of Large Language Models") for reproducibility. In this section, we mainly compare five different output formats. Specifically, Inline Bracketed and Inline XML represent an embedded paradigm where entity boundaries and types are inserted directly into the original sentence using brackets or XML tags, yielding natural-language-like outputs. The JSON-based formats treat NER as a structured information extraction task. Category-grouped JSON organizes entities by their label keys, which can only handle the entity-label relationship while ambiguity exists due to the lack of positional information. ###### Abstract

Named entity recognition (NER) is evolving from a sequence labeling task into a generative paradigm with the rise of large language models (LLMs). We conduct a systematic evaluation of open-source LLMs on both flat and nested NER tasks. We investigate several research questions including the performance gap between generative NER and traditional NER models, the impact of output formats, whether LLMs rely on memorization, and the preservation of general capabilities after fine-tuning. Through experiments across eight LLMs of varying scales and four standard NER datasets, we find that: (1) With parameter-efficient fine-tuning and structured formats like inline bracketed or XML, open-source LLMs achieve performance competitive with traditional encoder-based models and surpass closed-source LLMs like GPT-3; (2) The NER capability of LLMs stems from instruction-following and generative power, not mere memorization of entity-label pairs; and (3) Applying NER instruction tuning has minimal impact on general capabilities of LLMs, even improving performance on datasets like DROP due to enhanced entity understanding. These findings demonstrate that generative NER with LLMs is a promising, user-friendly alternative to traditional methods. We release the data

# ABSTRACT

Graph-based RAG organizes fragmented text into explicit knowledge structures for retrieval through entities, relations, and article summaries. However, directly bringing graph-based RAG to smartphones creates a mismatch between cloud-oriented graph methods and mobile constraints: compact on-device models are more likely to miss entities, predict incorrect relations, or merge distinct entity mentions, while multi-level graph summaries require frequent, large-context LLM invocations. We build [NAME C20], to the best of our knowledge, the first graph-based RAG framework end-to-end deployed on commercial smartphones. [NAME C20] combines MRGraph, a two-layer mobile graph that preserves entities, relations, and source paragraphs; EvoNER, which incrementally learns unseen entity types and locally updates the graph; and ATPlanner, which uses one LLM call to guide hybrid retrieval under a fixed budget. On real smartphones, [NAME C20] outperforms prior mobile RAG baselines by up to 22.4 points in correctness, constructs knowledge graphs 13.77× faster, and consumes only 1.36% of the energy compared with the latest lightweight methods. ## 2.2 PREVIOUS RAG METHODS

**Vector-based RAG** encodes document chunks into dense embeddings and retrieves the top-$k$ most similar chunks for each query (Karpukhin et al., 2020). This design scales well, but each chunk is retrieved independently which has no explicit mechanism to chain evidence across documents.

**Graph-based RAG** addresses this by extracting entities and relations from documents and organizing them into entity-relation graphs that make cross-document connections explicit (Edge et al., 2024; Peng et al., 2025). ## Abstract

Deploying large language models (LLMs) as personal assistants on mobile devices demands privacy, low latency, and offline availability, yet the computational cost of giant models clashes with strict edge-hardware budgets. We argue that this tension cannot be resolved by model compression alone; it requires decomposing on-device intelligence into complementary functional roles. We present SmartRAG, a fully on-device framework that organizes an intelligent assistant around four coordinated modules—Perception, Memory, Focus, and Thinking. At the core of SmartRAG is EvoNER, a continually learnable named-entity recognizer that incrementally expands its label inventory through teacher-distilled updates, enabling the system to absorb previously unseen entity types without retraining the backbone LLM. Extracted knowledge is stored

Although on-device RAG has recently achieved preliminary progress, most existing methods remain centered on naive vector retrieval—that is, relying on semantic similarity between queries and document snippets to facilitate memory access. While this paradigm is well-suited for handling problems involving local matching, it struggles to address complex queries that require cross-segment evidence aggregation, entity linking, and multi-step reasoning. To address this limitation, on-cloud RAG research has begun to leverage graph structures to enhance the retrieval process, explicitly modeling the connections between entities, relations, and evidence to improve multi-hop question-answering capabilities. However, the majority of existing graph-based RAG methods are built upon powerful models, relying heavily on models with tens of billions of parameters to execute critical steps such as graph construction, summarization, and relation organization. While this premise may hold true in cloud-based environments, it clearly fails in on-device scenarios: on-device systems simply cannot bear the computational, latency, energy, and cost overheads associated with models of such scale.

Based on this issue, we believe that the key to on-device RAG lies not in directly compressing c

Answering. The LLM generates responses conditioned on retrieved evidence, constrained to structured schemas that favor extractive grounding to reduce hallucination.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Setup

We use two compact LLM families in this work: Qwen3 [Qwen Team, 2025] and Ministral3 [Liu et al., 2026a]. Both are quantized to Q6_K via llama.cpp [Gerganov, 2023]. All offline one-time preparation, including quantization, LoRA training, and dataset pre-processing, is performed on a cloud server with two NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs, while the full online SmartRAG pipeline—memory ingestion, indexing, retrieval, and answer generation—runs entirely on-device. For multi-hop retrieval planning, we train a task-specific LoRA decomposer [Hu et al., 2022] on a self-constructed dataset derived from MultiHopQA and HotpotQA, where decomposition targets are generated offline using Claude Opus 4.6 and then filtered by rules with manual verification. The decomposer is used only to generate retrieval plans; final answers are always produced by the quantized backbone conditioned on retrieved evidence. All on-device experiments are conducted on two real smartphones: OnePlus 13 (Snapdragon 8 Elite, 16 GB RAM) and OnePlus 15 (Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, 16 GB RAM).

We evaluate on four QA benchma

**Why these baselines were not deployed as real-phone end-to-end systems.** Our goal in the baseline comparison is to evaluate answer quality under a matched compact-backbone regime, rather than to claim that every baseline is equally suitable for direct mobile deployment. The original formulations of InstructRAG, StableRAG, and TruthfulRAG introduce additional stages that make them difficult to treat as drop-in phone pipelines. InstructRAG explicitly denoises retrieved contents through self-synthesized rationales and supports both in-context learning (ICL) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). TruthfulRAG introduces additional KG-oriented processing steps, including knowledge-graph construction, graph retrieval, and entropy-based filtering. StableRAG emphasizes repeatability, frozen retrieval, and structured output normalization, with a pipeline that depends on OpenAI-style generation and embedding calls together with a persistent retrieval store. These original designs are meaningful in their intended settings, but they differ substantially from a single-pass compact on-device assistant stack. For this reason, we treat them as *reference RAG baselines evaluated under a matched backend and quantization setup*, rather than as directly deployable mobile systems.

### 3.1 Architecture overview

The SmartRAG architecture ([Figure 1](#S3.F1 "In 3.1 Architecture overview ‣ 3 Method ‣ SmartRAG: Native Graph-Based RAG for Mobile Device")) consists of four interacting modules. The Perception module transforms unstructured text into structured knowledge via EvoNER (an on-device NER component, [Section 3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Perception: EvoNER and entity discovery ‣ 3 Method ‣ SmartRAG: Native Graph-Based RAG for Mobile Device")) and a lightweight relation classifier, producing entity–relation triplets. The Memory module organizes these triplets into MRGraph, a persistent knowledge structure that binds entities and relations to their source paragraphs for provenance ([Section 3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Memory: MRGraph ‣ 3 Method ‣ SmartRAG: Native Graph-Based RAG for Mobile Device")). ## 1 Introduction

In recent years, as the application of large language models (LLMs) in real-world interactive tasks continues to deepen, memory is gradually emerging as a critical capability in LLM system determining whether the system can support long-term personalization, continuous knowledge updates, and contextually consistent reasoning. This issue is of particular significance for on-device scenarios, as the core value of such deployments lies precisely in data locality, privacy protection, and personalized services capabilities that inherently require the system to establish and maintain a local memory built around the user’s private data, device-local content, and environmental context. # SmartRAG: Native Graph-Based RAG for Mobile Device

###### Abstract

Deploying large language models (LLMs) as personal assistants on mobile devices demands privacy, low latency, and offline availability, yet the computational cost of giant models clashes with strict edge-hardware budgets. We argue that this tension cannot be resolved by model compression alone; it requires decomposing on-device intelligence into complementary functional roles. We present SmartRAG, a fully on-device framework that organizes an intelligent assistant around four coordinated modules—*Perception*, *Memory*, *Focus*, and *Thinking*. At the core of SmartRAG is EvoNER, a continually learnable named-entity recognizer that incrementally expands its label inventory through teacher-distilled updates, enabling the system to absorb previously unseen entity types without retraining the backbone LLM. Extracted knowledge is stored in MRGraph, a three-layer provenance-preserving knowledge graph, and retrieved at query time through a hybrid pipeline combining graph traversal, lexical matching, and dense semantic search. The on-device LLM is invoked only for high-value semantic operations—labeling, planning, and answer synthesis—keeping inference costs bounded. ## 5 Discussion and conclusion

We have presented SmartRAG, an on-device architecture for adaptive question answering that decomposes intelligence into four coordinated functional roles. By shifting continuous adaptation to efficient structured computation and reserving LLM inference for high-value semantic operations, SmartRAG achieves multi-hop reasoning performance competitive with substantially larger cloud-based models while running entirely on commodity smartphones.
## References

#### StableRAG.

StableRAG is a method designed to improve repeatability and robustness in RAG systems, mitigating retrieval-permutation-induced hallucinations through stable retrieval ordering and structured rendering. In our experiments, we retained the stability-oriented evaluation logic described in the original paper while replacing the original serving configuration with the same compact quantized backbones and llama.cpp backend used in the rest of the paper. As with TruthfulRAG and InstructRAG, we treat the resulting system as a *simulated reference implementation under matched inference conditions*, not as a true smartphone deployment. This distinction is important because StableRAG is primarily designed to study response stability and retrieval repeatability, whereas SmartRAG is optimized for persistent structured memory and end-to-end on-device execution.

#### Named entity recognition and continual learning.

Span-based NER ([Yu et al., 2020](#bib.bib20); [Fu et al., 2021](#bib.bib21)) formulates entity detection as span classification over enumerated candidates, avoiding the label dependency of sequential taggers. Continual learning for NER ([Monaikul et al., 2021](#bib.bib10)) addresses the challenge of absorbing new entity types without forgetting old ones, commonly using knowledge distillation ([Hinton et al., 2015](#bib.bib9)) or regularization ([Kirkpatrick et al., 2017](#bib.bib8)). Our EvoNER combines span-based detection with a reserved-label classifier and teacher-distilled incremental updates, specifically designed for on-device expansion of the entity vocabulary.
